title: The Audience Mindsets Education Brands Can Reach with Premium Content
summary: Education audiences bring specific mindsets to what they watch. See how premium content helps your brand meet them in the right one.
body_markdown:
In the fall of 2000, CBS premiered a procedural drama about a Las Vegas forensics team that set the country aflame: CSI: Crime Scene Investigation. It flipped the classic tropes of TV police procedurals on its head, swapping beat cops and brooding detectives for lab techs and investigators processing scientific evidence to solve the case-of-the-week.


Within a few years, colleges noticed something they likely never saw coming. There was a measurable rise in students choosing to major in forensic science, and a wave of new degree programs created to meet the demand. At[West Virginia University](https://www.mccrone.com/mm/csi-effect-forensic-microscopy/) , forensic science became the school’s most popular undergraduate major within four years of the show’s premiere, drawing 13% of that fall’s incoming class. Researchers named the pattern the CSI Effect, and[a 2006 study](https://pubs.acs.org/jceda8/article/83/5/690/3506206/Teaching-To-Avoid-the-CSI-Effect-Keeping-the-Science-in-Forensic-Science) documented the same rise in student interest playing out in classrooms nationwide.


It’s usually told as a forensic-science curiosity, a fluke of one show’s timing. Treated as a case study instead, it says something bigger about how premium content can move an entire vertical of advertisers, even when they have nothing to do with crime labs.


Education spans more than one audience. A university trying to fill its incoming class and a school supplies brand trying to reach parents before the first day back are chasing entirely different purchase decisions. Their timelines don’t line up, and neither does what’s triggering the decision on screen. Two distinct mindsets sit inside this one vertical, and each needs premium content to do a different job.


## The Behavior


### The Someday Mindset


Watching someone competent do a job on screen lets a viewer try on that identity before committing to it in real life. This is the mechanism behind the CSI Effect, and it isn’t limited to crime dramas. It extends to other genres as well. A[2025 systematic review](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10384162251345578) examining the link between media and career choice found that shows like Grey’s Anatomy and ER have measurably shaped students’ opinions of STEM and medical careers, in some cases directly influencing their choice of study.


Media functions as a introduction to careers someone might not otherwise picture themselves in, and premium content built around expertise or a specific professional skill set puts a brand in front of those viewers as they begin to consider their future careers.


### The Fresh Start Effect


A completely different mechanism drives the other half of this vertical. Behavioral researchers Hengchen Dai, Katherine Milkman, and Jason Riis published[a 2014 study in Management Science](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/mnsc.2014.1901) establishing what they called the fresh start effect: temporal landmarks, among them the outset of a new semester, measurably spike people’s motivation toward self-improvement and reinvention. It’s the same instinct behind a New Year’s resolution, just triggered by a different date on the calendar.


Back-to-school is one of the most universal fresh-start landmarks there is, and the spending data backs up how seriously people treat it.[The National Retail Federation](https://nrf.com/media-center/press-releases/majority-of-back-to-school-shoppers-get-a-head-start-on-the-season) projected a record $146.8 billion in combined back-to-school and back-to-college spending in 2026, up from $128.2 billion in 2025, and 62% of shoppers had already started buying before the season even officially opened. That reset doesn’t stay a mindset. It shows up as a shopping list, whether its new school supplies or a first-day fit.


## Premium Content Geared Towards the Someday Mindset


### Medical dramas


**What it is:** Shows like The Pitt and ER, where the hospital floor is a pressure cooker and the people inside it are the only thing holding it together.


**The viewer posture:** Viewers are watching a specific kind of competence: staying calm, reading a room, making the right call under pressure. That’s a transferable skill set, the kind of thing a viewer can picture building for themselves.


**Why it works for education:** This tracks directly with the research on media and medical career interest —[the same 2025 review](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10384162251345578) that names Grey’s Anatomy and ER as measurable influences on STEM career perception. Nursing programs, medical assistant certification, healthcare administration degrees, and EMT training all have a natural home here.


### Crime & legal procedurals


**What it is:** Shows like CSI and the Law & Order, where the case gets cracked because someone in a lab coat or a courtroom knew exactly what to look for.


**The viewer posture:** This is the genre that established the CSI Effect, and the pull is the same one that drove real enrollment. When someone watches an expert solve a puzzle in real time, they feel inspired to learn how to do it themselves.


**Why it works for education:** Criminal justice degrees, forensic science programs, paralegal certificates, and cybersecurity bootcamps are the most direct match in this collection, backed by the same enrollment data tied to this exact genre.


### Competition & culinary shows


**What it is:** Shows like Chopped and Beat Bobby Flay, where viewers get a first hand look at how some of the most delicious dishes in the world are made.


**The viewer posture:** The format itself is pure entertainment for foodies, but it’s also somewhat instructional. Viewers watch and learn how dishes are prepared almost in real time, which shifts their mindset from “I could never do that” to “I could actually learn that.”


**Why it works for education:** Culinary schools, trade certification programs, and hospitality management degrees fit naturally here.


## Premium Content Geared Towards the Fresh Start Effect


### Home renovation & makeover shows


**What it is:** Shows like Property Brothers, Love It or List It, and Home Town, where people are searching for a new house, or a way to turn a tired space into something that fits the person living there.


**The viewer posture:** This is the fresh-start impulse applied to a physical space. A dorm room is often the first space someone gets to decorate entirely on their own terms, and this genre primes viewers to see a blank room as an opportunity rather than a chore.


**Why it works for education:** Dorm and apartment furnishing brands have a clear stake in this genre.[The NRF](https://nrf.com/media-center/press-releases/majority-of-back-to-school-shoppers-get-a-head-start-on-the-season) puts total dorm and apartment furnishing spend at $14 billion in 2026, averaging $194 per college student, making it one of the single largest back-to-college categories after electronics.


### School-set teen dramas


**What it is:** Shows like Pretty Little Liars, Gossip Girl, and One Tree Hill, where a character’s wardrobe does as much storytelling as the plot, and a new school year often doubles as the moment a character reintroduces themselves.


**The viewer posture:** Reinvention through clothing is baked into the format. Every new season starts with someone stepping back into the hallway as a slightly different version of who they were last semester.


**Why it works for education:** Back-to-school apparel brands have a strong data case here.[The NRF](https://nrf.com/media-center/press-releases/majority-of-back-to-school-shoppers-get-a-head-start-on-the-season) reports K-12 families spending an average of $250.29 on clothing and accessories this year ($12.5 billion total), while college families average $182.39 ($13.1 billion total).


### School-set workplace comedy


**What it is:** Abbott Elementary, set inside the exact kind of building the products in this bucket are headed for.


**The viewer posture:** This one runs on contextual alignment rather than aspiration. The setting does the work without needing a transformation arc.


**Why it works for education:** General school supply brands get the most literal placement available in this collection. K-12 families are projected to spend $146.45 on average on school supplies alone this year ($7.3 billion total), inside a[broader K-12 back-to-school total of $43.3 billion](https://nrf.com/media-center/press-releases/majority-of-back-to-school-shoppers-get-a-head-start-on-the-season) .


## The Premium Play


Someday Mindset content earns the most from a long runway, the same way[travel content](https://research.mountain.com/insights/travel-brands-can-win-the-inspiration-window-with-premium-content/) does. Enrollment decisions form months ahead of an application deadline, and a viewer who’s considering a nursing career or a forensics major in October is worth reaching well before spring admissions decisions land.


Fresh Start Effect content runs on a shorter, more compressed calendar, but that calendar starts earlier than marketers may have traditionally assumed. With[62% of shoppers](https://nrf.com/media-center/press-releases/majority-of-back-to-school-shoppers-get-a-head-start-on-the-season) already buying before the season officially opens, summer placement carries more weight than an August-only push would suggest.


The CSI Effect was a happy accident for colleges. It wasn’t a one-time fluke, either. Medical dramas have already shown the same shift playing out again, in a completely different field. Education brands don’t need an accident of their own for the mechanism to work; it already does. Viewers are forming that interest every time they watch. The only variable left is whether your ad budget is there when they do.
